what: coverage
was: «Every Queensland Falco belongs to one household in the Burdekin cane country» — on Searched, from a FindMyPast sweep
now: Every Queensland Falco IN FINDMYPAST does. Queensland's own index holds four more: Carminantonio, Filomena, their son Raffaele and their daughter Costanza, all registered at Brisbane.
how: The Queensland BDM historical index searched directly, surname by surname, rather than through a subscription site's re-hosting of it.
why: The sentence read as a statement about Queensland and was only ever a statement about one supplier's holdings. Left standing it would have told the next reader that the Brisbane family was unregistered, which is the opposite of the truth — and it would have hidden four registration numbers that make certificates orderable.
by: a direct sweep of the state index, prompted by asking which free sources had never been tried

what: identification
was: Raffaele Falco at Nudgee, V-0946 — «PROBABLY the son of Carminantonio & Filomena b. 1925 at Benevento»
now: His son, documented. The Queensland death registration of 28 September 1988 names his parents as Carmine Antonio Falco and Filomena Anechina.
how: Queensland BDM historical index, registration 1988/8547.
why: The cemetery gave a plot and an interment date but no parents, so the join rested on a first name, a burial date and a plausible age. A state registration that names both parents is a different order of evidence, and it happens to agree.
by: the parent columns of the Queensland index

what: dates
was: Costanza Falco (Crisci) — a bare name, no birth, no death, no country
now: Born about 1928; died in Queensland on 1 July 1965, at about thirty-seven. Registration 1965/B/74373 names her parents as Carmine Antonio Falco and Filomena Annechina.
how: Queensland BDM historical index, found under her married surname Crisci rather than under Falco.
why: She was the one child of that household the archive could say nothing about at all — and the reason is that she married and the index files her as a Crisci. It also places her in Australia, which nothing here had done.
by: sweeping married surnames as well as birth surnames

what: reading
was: «MARIA CARFORA», a seventy-year-old of Arienzo, 1838 atto 77
now: MARIA CARBONE, widow of Saverio Carfora
how: Re-read at 3400 px. She is a Carbone; the Carfora was her husband.
why: Maria Carfora is the single name this archive most wants to find — the probable mother of Filomena Annecchino. Unchecked it would have put a Maria Carfora born about 1768 into the Arienzo register, a century and a province away from Forchia, for someone to join to generation seven one day.
by: a zoom, prompted by the reading being the one I hoped for

what: reading
was: «MARIA CARFORA», an eighty-year-old of Arienzo, 1837 atto 27
now: MARTA CARFORA, wife of Domenico Cioffi
how: Re-read at 3400 px.
why: THE SAME MISTAKE, IN TWO VOLUMES, ONE DAY APART. Twice the eye supplied the name it was hunting. That is no longer an anecdote about handwriting — it is a measured property of the person reading, and it is why the archive now zooms every reading that is the one it hoped for.
by: the same check, applied because the first failure had been written down

what: reading
was: «DOMENICA FALCO», wife of Raffaele Cioffi, published from the 1843 register
now: FRANCESCA FALCO
how: Corrected by TWO independent readings — the 1840 and 1842 volumes — not one.
why: The 1843 file had published «Domenica» as an explicitly flagged hypothesis. Three acts, three clerks, one spelling of her name.

what: reading
was: «Suor ELENA GIULIA MIGLIORE», read as a nun's name in the 1843 register
now: GIULIA MIGLIORE — the word is PLENA, part of «Ave Gratia Plena», the hospital's name
how: The phrase «Ospedale di Ave Gratia Plena» recurs in 1837, 1839, 1840 and 1842, which is what exposed it.
why: A hospital was misread as a person. It is the clearest case in the archive of a phrase being mistaken for a name.

what: reading
was: «RAFFAELE FALCO, thirteen», dead 1838 atto 71
now: PASQUALE FALCO, thirteen, son of Francesco Falco and Gasparda Falco
how: Re-read at 3400 px.
why: Generation four IS a Raffaele Falco born in 1818. A misread Raffaele dying in 1838 would have looked like a catastrophe for the line. It is a different child of a different household entirely.
by: a zoom on a Falco act, as the rule requires

what: reading
was: ANGELO MORGILLO, «ninety-two», widower of «Marta Grieco», 1838 atto 24
now: ANGELO MORGILLO, NINETY, widower of MARIA RIVETTI
how: Re-read at 3400 px on the same plate.
why: The wife's surname matters: Morgillo and Rivetti are the two surnames that flank this line, and here they are married to each other a generation before the founding couple's children.

what: reading
was: ANGELO DIGLIO aged SIXTY at 1837 atto 11 and SEVENTY four days later at atto 12
now: SEVENTY in both — the ten-year jump was my eye, not the clerk's
how: Both acts re-read at 3400 px.
why: It would have been the single most spectacular age in the archive. It was a misreading, and saying so is worth more than the anecdote would have been.
by: a zoom on a claim that was too good

what: claim
was: ANTONIO BERNARDO offered as «the useful counter-case» for the register's ages — 70, 76, 70, 70, three of four agreeing
now: WITHDRAWN. The 1837 volume makes him FIFTY-THREE in June, eight months before the first of those seventies, on a different street.
how: Read at 3400 px, 1837 atto 52.
why: An argument published yesterday was refuted by today's volume. Either there are two Antonio Bernardo or one man aged seventeen years in eight months. The 1838 note is corrected in place rather than deleted, because the argument was published.

what: claim
was: «The register is internally consistent inside a volume and only falls apart between volumes»
now: Nearly right, and now stated properly. Across six appearances in 1837 the hospital pair read: Diglio 70 six times out of six; Migliore 58 five times and 54 once. Eleven of twelve agree.
how: Counting every appearance instead of two.
why: The first version was an overstatement built on two acts. The corrected version is the sharpest thing the sweeps can say about the ages — and it took four volumes read end to end to be able to say it.

what: reading
was: 1838 atto 15 dated «il dì VENTINOVE del mese di Febbrajo»
now: 24 February. 1838 was not a leap year.
how: THE ARITHMETIC caught it, not a second opinion. At 3200 px the word is not «ventinove»; the neighbouring acts bracket it.
why: A date that cannot exist is the cheapest error-detector this archive has, and it only works if the failures are written down.

what: reading
was: GIUSEPPE DI GUIDA, «ninety-five», 1837 atto 33
now: NINETY-ONE — and his widow's surname LEFT BLANK on purpose
how: At 3400 px the surname will not resolve between Diretti, di Ruggio and Rivetti.
why: Two of those are names this archive is actively hunting. Having twice today written down the name it hoped for, it recorded a blank instead. Recording a blank is cheaper than recording a wish.
by: the lesson of the same morning

what: identification
was: Generation three's wife published as ANDREANA CRISCI
now: UNDECIDED. The 1839 act naming their daughter Filomena reads ANDRIANA CIOFFI, verified twice at 3000 and 3400 px.
how: Both readings now stand. Either two men called Vincenzo Falco, or one of the two acts is misread.
why: This archive has already been caught by exactly this pair of shapes — five years of «Cossi» turned out to be «Cioffi». Settling it needs Raffaele Falco's act re-read and, if it can be found, the marriage.

what: code
was: GIUSEPPA FERRARO filed in the register under MARIA, her middle name
now: Filed under FERRARO
how: FERRARO is both the Zampiello maternal surname and the Italian for a blacksmith. The builder stripped trailing trade words blind and ate the surname. The registers settle it: in 555 of 568 rows a trade follows a comma and a surname does not.
why: Maria Rosa Ferraro went to ROSA and Antonio Ferraro to ANTONIO. The surname filter was offering forenames. Junk surname buckets: 24 to 1.

what: privacy
was: GENERATION NINE — living, born 1955 — published with her birth date on her person page; generation eight likewise on the direct-line page
now: Both masked. Living people carry a name and a relationship and nothing else.
how: The person-graph builder decided redaction using a predicate that excluded ANCESTORS. That belongs in the living-relatives roster, where an ancestor is rightly not a relative — but ancestry has nothing to do with whether someone is alive, and the wife's own mother is both.
why: It is the exact leak the direct-line page had been fixed for once already. Verified after: no living record carries a date, place or event; no living person's node shows a year.
by: checking whether Carmine Falco could be published at all

what: reading
was: Five years of «COSSI» in this archive
now: CIOFFI
how: The 1825 register shows the two shapes side by side in one hand.
why: The founding misreading of this archive, and the reason every ambiguous surname since has been left visibly undecided. One Crisci household is STILL unsettled for the same reason — «Marcello Crisci» in 1823 and «Marcello Cossi» in 1828, with the identical wife.
by: reading the volume act by act

what: identification
was: AGOSTINO FALCONE at the head of the line
now: MATTEO FALCO — and Falcone discarded
how: The registers name Matteo Falco as the father in three separate children's death acts.
why: The family tree STILL carries Agostino Falcone as generation two's father. He is drawn on Pasquale Falco's page struck through and labelled superseded, beside the man who replaced him. Corrections here are not deleted.

what: a dead end that was not one
was: “The file for marriage act 26 (Falco × Crisci) is not in the 1814 processetti. Do not search these two again.”
now: It was there — bundle 16, images 265–274 — and it is the richest document this archive has found.
how: An earlier session worked the volume from the back, found a publication act numbered 25 dated 20 November 1814 and then the 1815 divider, and concluded the volume stopped short of act 26. But processetti BUNDLES are numbered in their own sequence, in the order the banns were published — not by the number the marriage later received in the marriage register. The 1814 volume holds SEVENTEEN bundles; Vincenzo and Adriana published in September and married in December, so their file is bundle 16 while their marriage is act 26. The «25» that stopped the earlier search was a publication act number inside bundle 17, the last of the year.
why: This is the most expensive kind of error an archive can make — a wrong negative, written down as a rule, that stops anyone looking again. It stayed in QUEUE.md under “Dead ends, recorded so they are not repeated” for weeks. The standing rule is now: in a processetti volume match on names and publication date, never on the marriage act number — and every “do not search again” note must carry the reasoning that produced it, so the reasoning can be checked.

what: a birth date
was: Vincenzo Falco, generation three, born 1793
now: Baptised 1 February 1792 — and christened Vincenzo RAFFAELE
how: His own baptism extract, copied from the parish register (liber IX, fol. 47v) by the archpriest Giacinto Morgillo on 13 September 1814 and filed in his marriage dossier.
why: 1793 came from his marriage act's stated age of 21, which was itself wrong. The date is corrected, and the old one is left standing here because the seven-way age conflict it caused is one of the most-cited things on this site. Knowing the real date does not erase the conflict — it explains it.

what: a surname conflict, closed
was: Generation three's wife published two ways — Andreana CRISCI, and Andriana CIOFFI from the 1839 death register
now: CRISCI. Baptised ADRIANA on 30 November 1796, daughter of Arcangelo Crisci and Sara Ruggiero.
how: Six documents of 1814 — the dossier cover sheet, both notarial consent acts, both civil banns, and her own baptism extract — all say Crisci, and four of them name her parents.
why: The 1839 reading was published as a live conflict rather than suppressed, and it stays visible here. It was either the clerk's error or mine. The baptism also explains the variants: Adriana at the font becomes Andreana, Andriana and Andrea in the registers. They are one woman.

what: a death bracket, narrowed
was: Matteo Falco dead by 17 October 1822 — the earliest act that calls him defunto
now: Dead by 8 December 1814
how: A notarial act of that date names «Pasquale Falco del FU Matteo». Nothing published was wrong; the window simply closes almost eight years earlier.
why: Recorded here because this site publishes the narrowing of a claim as readily as its overturning. The bracket on Matteo's death is now [1786, 8 Dec 1814].

what: a correction, corrected
was: This page said, hours earlier on the same day: “Bundle 25's publication is dated 20 November, two months later than ours.”
now: There is no bundle 25. The 1814 volume holds seventeen bundles. The «25» was a publication act number inside bundle 17.
how: Sweeping all 290 images of the volume as contact sheets and reading every bundle cover. Each is headed «Numero N — Comune Corpo d'Arienzo»; they run 1 to 17, and bundle 17 is Francesco Crisci fu Alessandro × Teresa Morgillo, published 20 November 1814.
why: I repeated a number out of the earlier session's note while writing the correction that overturned that very note — without checking it. The mechanism I described was right and is unchanged; the illustration was wrong. It is published because a correction that quietly acquires its own errors is worse than no correction, and because this is exactly the failure the same day's other entry warns about: a figure inherited rather than verified.

what: a diagram that misled
was: The Lines diagram drew the ZAMPIELLO as a separate stream running alongside this family, omitted SAN FELICE A CANCELLO and FORCHIA as places entirely, and used one visual grammar — a dot on a lane — for places, for people, and once for a ship.
now: A place-spine. The Zampiello, Annecchino and Morgillo are drawn JOINING the line at the generation and town where they join. Names sit under the place they belong to.
how: Checked the diagram's places against places.json and the atlas. It showed seven places; it was missing San Felice a Cancello — where Angela Rosa Morgillo, generation four's wife, was born — and never drew Forchia as the Annecchino's town even though that marriage is the reason generation eight was born there. Two of the five lanes had people, not places, as their nodes, and one had the ship Sydney.
why: The Zampiello error was the worst of it: drawn as a parallel river, they read as a different family being compared with this one, when Francesca Zampiello married Carmine Falco in 1955 and from generation eight onward they ARE this family. A diagram that is wrong is worse than no diagram, because nobody checks a picture against the prose. Raised by David, who spotted all three faults from the image alone.

what: an age, and a striking claim that rested on it
was: Andreana Crisci “married at about sixteen” — inferred from her stated age of twenty in her son's 1818 birth act, which implied a birth about 1798.
now: She was born 30 November 1796 and married at EIGHTEEN. The 1818 act understates her by about a year and a half.
how: Her baptism extract in the 1814 marriage dossier. The 1818 birth act was then re-read at native resolution: it does say «venti», twenty, and it does say «ANDREANA CRISCI» — the surname is unambiguous, which settles the 1839 «Cioffi» reading a second way.
why: “Married at sixteen” is the kind of detail a reader remembers and repeats, and it was this archive's own inference from a clerk's guess rather than anything a record said. Eighteen is still young. The same act gets her husband's age right — twenty-seven, when he was twenty-six and three months, which is correct by the year-a-man-is-in reckoning these clerks used. Right about him, wrong about her, in one sentence.

what: an uncertain reading, resolved
was: The apothecary's mother recorded as «LUCIA COPPA(?)/CIOFFI» — read at 3400px and left with a question mark and an alternative.
now: LUCIA CIOFFI. Read at native resolution: «e di Lucia Cioffi Defunta».
how: Re-fetching the act as a IIIF region at the image's own resolution rather than scaling the whole leaf. The double-f ligature is unmistakable at full size and was not at 3400px.
why: A name carried with a question mark for weeks is a name nobody can search for. It also changes what the record means: CIOFFI is a gentry surname at Arienzo, and in February 1815 a Don Saverio CIOFFI was married to a Donna Anna Maria RIVETTI. The two families married in both directions.

what: a town recorded as unreachable that was never searched for
was: “San Felice a Cancello is a separate comune with its own registers, NONE OF WHICH THIS ARCHIVE HAS READ.” San Felice is where generation four's wife, Angela Rosa Morgillo, was born.
now: Its registers are on Antenati and have been all along — Archivio di Stato di Caserta, marriages from 1809 at an_ua50221. The 1817 marriages have now been read.
why: The wording said “has not read” and was heard, including by me, as “cannot read”. In fact nobody had looked. It was missed because Antenati catalogues the town under its older name, «San Felice (oggi San Felice a Cancello)», and because this archive reached Antenati by guessing arks from an arithmetic rule derived by hand for Arienzo alone — a method that can only ever find what it already knows about.
how: A search endpoint that returns ark ids in plain HTML: search-registry/?localita=<town>. Resolving those arks gives the series arithmetic for any town. The archive's own survey covers five Valle Caudina towns and does not include San Felice at all.

what: a living person's birth date, published — for the third time
was: The rebuilt Lines diagram printed generation nine's FULL DATE OF BIRTH beside her name, under the heading BORN HERE — on /lines and, because the home page embeds the same figure, on the front page of the site. She is living.
now: «9 · Giuseppina Falco — living — named only», under the heading LIVING. The 1955 on the Benevento stop now belongs to generation eight's marriage, where it is a fact about two people who are dead.
how: Sweeping the built site for the date and finding it in the raw HTML of two pages. The visible text of /direct-line was correct; the diagram was not.
why: This archive has now leaked this exact birth year THREE times: once through a redaction function reused from the wrong place, once through the timeline's geometry — and now through a diagram I built myself on the day this correction was written, hours after re-reading the standing rule. Textual fixes have not held, so THE FIX IS STRUCTURAL: the diagram now looks every date up against the person graph and prints «living — named only» instead, whatever the underlying data says. Data can be wrong; the guard cannot be bypassed by editing a string. And this entry had to be written twice: the first version QUOTED THE DATE IT WAS CORRECTING, which republished it on a page nobody would think to check. The release gate caught that on its first run. A correction must describe a leak without reproducing it.
by: auditing the built HTML, not the source

what: a search recorded as promising that was not
was: Orazio Morgillo × Vincenza Pesce would be found in the San Felice marriage registers of 1816 or 1817.
now: Neither year holds them. Both volumes have been read act by act and the couple is not in either.
how: San Felice a Cancello, Matrimoni 1817 (an_ua50229, 22 images) and 1816 (an_ua50228, 26 images), swept in full.
why: Published as a negative so the two years are not read again. The couple was reached anyway, and by a better route: their daughter's BIRTH act, which names both parents outright. The lesson is recorded on /morgillo — when the target is a couple and a child's date is known, go to the birth register, because a birth act names both parents and a marriage act has to be found first. The marriage is still open; the remaining window is San Felice 1813-1815, or another parish if Vincenza was not of the town.

what: a probable identification, now established
was: «Almost certainly the same woman, married in 1814 and buried before the winter was out. Published as PROBABLE, not proved.»
now: Established. Bundle 13 carries Margarita Crisci's own baptism extract — «nata ex ANGELO CRISCI et GRAZIA, 27 September 1780» — and the death extracts of both those parents. The 1815 death act names the same two parents, both dead. It is the same woman.
how: Reading inside the bundle rather than only its cover. A processetto had to carry death certificates for any dead parent or grandparent, so it also yielded her grandfather: THOMAS CRISCI, widower, dead 21 March 1789 aged forty-six.
why: Recorded because the archive published it as probable the same day and can now say why it is not. The groom's surname is STILL not proved — the cover gives him only as «Angelo figlio di Nicola» — so that half stays open.

what: a hundred finding aids recorded as non-existent
was: «No index, no indice decennale, no marginal surnames — all three checked and absent. ~90 acts/year, ~1,350 total. ONE SCREENSHOT PER ACT.» That recipe governed twenty-eight years of death-register sweeps.
now: Antenati lists 100 INDEX VOLUMES for Arienzo alone — 39 for deaths, 44 for marriages, 17 for «diversi» — and 79 more for San Felice a Cancello. Arienzo death indexes run 1809 = an_ua14271, +1 per year, verified at 1818, 1828 and 1834. Each is ONE TO FOUR IMAGES and lists every death of the year with BOTH PARENTS NAMED.
how: Reading the catalogue's own facet list instead of paging the volumes. The facet is spelled «Morti, indice» and «Matrimoni, processetti» — query for «Processetti» alone and you get nothing, which is part of how this was missed.
why: This is the third wrong negative of the same shape in a single day — the 1814 processetto «not in the volume», San Felice «unread», and now indexes «absent». Each came from checking once, concluding, and writing the conclusion down as a rule that stopped anyone looking again. The acts are still worth reading for what an index omits — street, hour, declarants, the «parente» wording this archive's best finds turn on — but the register is no longer the place to START. Two cautions are published with it: the sort order changes year to year, and the scans are not always complete, so an absence in an index is not a negative.

what: a date, misread as a shorter word
was: Chiara Rivetti died on 3 SEPTEMBER 1843. Published on /rivetti, /direct-line and in the memory of this project, and used to date the widowhood that brackets Pasquale Falco's death.
now: 13 SEPTEMBER 1843. The act says «il dì TREDICI del mese di Settembre» in its heading and «nel giorno TREDICI … alle ore venti» in the declaration — twice. TREDICI was read as TRE.
how: The 1843 death INDEX, found the same day, gives «Rivetti Chiara … 13 7bre 1843». The act was then re-read at native resolution and says thirteen in both places.
why: It also removes an oddity nobody had questioned: the parish buried her on 16 September, which is a strange thirteen-day wait after a death on the 3rd and an ordinary three-day one after the 13th. THIS IS THE INDEX METHOD EARNING ITS KEEP ON ITS FIRST CONTROL TEST — it was run against a known answer precisely to see whether it could be trusted, and it caught an error in the known answer.

what: two witnesses given the wrong surname
was: «Two CIOFFI of strada Camellara walked to the town hall to report it.»
now: LUCA COSSI, 33, a SARTORE, and GIOVANNI COSSI, 43, a contadino — both of strada Camellara. Cossi, not Cioffi.
how: Re-reading the act at native resolution. Cossi is short with a double-s; Cioffi is longer and carries the -ffi ligature. At the resolution the plate was cropped to, they are not distinguishable.
why: Both are common Arienzo surnames and both appear all over this archive, so the confusion will recur. Recorded with the tell: at plate resolution you cannot separate them — go to the image.

what: a death bracket, narrowed by a negative
was: Matteo Falco, head of the line: dead by 8 December 1814, with 1786 to 1814 open.
now: Dead BEFORE 1809 — proved, not probable. Which puts his death in the parish register and nowhere else.
how: The Arienzo death indexes for 1809-1814, read in a fraction of the time the registers would take. No Matteo Falco of the founder's generation is in them.
why: Published because a negative that moves a bracket is worth as much as a positive, and because it redirects the search. All six index volumes for 1809-1814 have now been read PAGE FOR PAGE — the first pass left three years partial and the claim was published as «probable» until they were finished. Taken with the marriage indexes, which also begin in 1809, BOTH of Matteo Falco's vital events lie outside the civil series: his marriage of about 1760-66 and his death are in the parish books of Sant'Andrea or nowhere.

what: a namesake that will mislead the next searcher
was: Nothing published — this is a trap set for the future rather than an error corrected.
now: A MATTEO FALCO died at Arienzo on 28 August 1809 AGED FIFTEEN, and he is NOT the head of this line. The act reads «è morto MATTEO FALCO — di [ANNI struck, MESI written over it] QUINDICI» — the clerk corrected himself between years and months, and on either reading the deceased is a child.
how: The act itself, Arienzo Morti 1809 (an_ua14311, img 40 right), read at native resolution. The 1809 INDEX names his parents «Giuseppe, ed Antonia di [Guida]» without «fu», so both were living; the act gives the age the index omits. The Falco who died three days later, NICOLA, was likewise a child — «d'anni DUE», of strada Camellara.
why: Anyone searching «Matteo Falco death Arienzo» lands on this record, and it is exactly the shape of a find that looks like the answer. The founder was born about 1740 and had children baptised from 1767; he would have been sixty-nine in 1809. Published as a trap disarmed rather than an error corrected.

what: a suspicion, promoted to a document
was: «GIOACCHINO FALCO is a strong candidate for a fifth child of Matteo and Francesca, THOUGH NO RECORD YET NAMES HIS PARENTS.» Carried that way for years, and he sat among the people this archive could join to nobody.
now: «7. FALCO GIOACCHINO | Arienzo | CONTADINO | FALCO MATTEO, e CRISCI FRANCESCA | 14 Febrajo» — Arienzo deaths 1851. He is a documented son of the founding couple, who now have FIVE named children.
how: The alphabetical index bound at the front of the 1851 death register — four images. Not a register read act by act.
why: Recorded because the archive was RIGHT and refused to say so without a record. The suspicion rested on an inference from 1816, when Gioacchino and Giuseppe Falco declared the death of Crescenzo Rivetti as «parenti del defunto», Crescenzo being married to their sister Angela. Holding that as a candidate rather than a fact for years was the correct call, and this is what it looks like when the discipline pays.

what: two readings that disagreed, reconciled — and one of them was mine
was: The bride of Luigi Falco's 1815 marriage recorded two ways: «[C]ecilia VECCHIO» from the bundle cover, and «[?]ietta RENCHIELLO» from the marriage act. Published as an unresolved disagreement.
now: «[F]ietta VECCHILLO», eighteen, a filatrice of strada del Borgo, daughter of the late SABBATINO. The SURNAME is settled — Vecchillo is the cover's Vecchio in a fuller spelling. RENCHIELLO was my misreading and never existed.
how: Re-reading the marriage act at native resolution instead of from a composite strip.
why: Recorded because the archive published a disagreement between two sources when in fact one source had been read badly. The forename is STILL uncertain — «Fietta» against «Cecilia», and Fietta may be a contraction of Felicetta — so that half stays open and is marked as such.

what: my own headline claim, wrongly framed
was: «GIOVANNA FALCO, died 15 December 1812, daughter of Pasquale Falco and Chiara Rivetti — A DAUGHTER OF GENERATION TWO THIS ARCHIVE DID NOT HAVE.» Published on /direct-line, /searched and in the commit that announced the index method's first big find.
now: A SECOND daughter of that name. This archive already held a GIOVANNA FALCO who died on 15 SEPTEMBER 1805, daughter of the same parents, from the Arienzo parish register (FamilySearch 3Q9M-CSMY-B743-H). The 1812 Giovanna is a second child given her dead sister's name.
how: Querying the archive's own register for every Falco death before publishing further on the same family — which is what should have happened BEFORE the claim, not after.
why: The find is still real and still new: a second Giovanna, dying in 1812, is a child nobody had. But «a child this archive did not have» was the wrong sentence, and it was the most quotable sentence in the entry. The naming pattern it actually illustrates is one this archive has documented repeatedly — two Raffaele, two Pasquale, two Maria, and now two Giovanna. THE LESSON: a new find must be checked against what is already held, in the same pass that publishes it. Searching the register takes seconds; the claim stood for an hour.

what: an open question answered, and a namesake that is not a stranger after all
was: Raised the same morning: «One Giuseppe Falco married twice, or two Giuseppe Falco at Arienzo?» — 1809 gave two Falco children of a Giuseppe with different mothers, Antonia di Guida and Gelsomina Vigliotta. And the Matteo Falco who died 28 August 1809 was published as «a child of ANOTHER HOUSEHOLD».
now: TWO Giuseppe Falco, distinguished by street and wife — and the 1809 Matteo IS the founder's own grandson. PROVED the same day, not merely probable.
how: Two birth acts already in this archive settle it. «25 Nov 1816, strada COSTA: Giuseppe Falco, 36, MASSARO DI CAMPO, e GELSOMINA VIGLIOTTA» and «7 Jun 1818, strada CAMELLARA: Giuseppe Falco, 36, CONTADINO, e ANTONIA DI GUIDA». So the Matteo Falco who died at fifteen months on 28 August 1809 is not a stranger who happens to share the name: he is MATTEO FALCO'S GRANDSON, carrying his grandfather's name, and he died while his grandfather was still alive. The trap entry stands — he is still not the founder — but «another household» was wrong. Held as PROBABLE: it rests on street, trade, period and this archive's existing identification of Giuseppe, not on an act that says «fu Matteo» and «Antonia di Guida» in the same line. — AND IT IS NOW PROVED. A parish marriage act found hours later reads «JOSEPHUM FALCO FILIUM MATTHEI, e FRANCISCE CRISCI et ANTONIAM DI GUIDA filiam JOSEPHI e MAGDALENE», about August 1802. Giuseppe Falco of strada Camellara, husband of Antonia di Guida, is documented as Matteo's son in the same act that marries him. The infant Matteo of 1809 is his child and the founder's grandson.

what: another age taken from a death act, corrected by a baptism
was: Chiara Rivetti «di anni OTTANTA» at her death on 13 September 1843, and so born about 1763.

what: a mother's surname that two document series do not agree on

what: a child this archive never knew existed, and a name explained

how: Arienzo parish baptisms, the 1774 leaf, read from the image.

what: a negative produced by searching the wrong collection

how: Arienzo, Morti 1846, atto 39, read from the image after the index pointed at it.
why: Two small things that are really one thing. **The index is a finding aid and never a source** — it has now been caught on an act number and a month in a single year. And the ages in these acts are estimates: this is the cleanest example the archive has, one man given the same age three years apart, in a series it once used to date births.

what: a third Michele Falco, and a household not previously held

how: Arienzo, Morti 1846, atto 39, found through the annual death index.
why: Recorded because a name identifies nobody in this town and the archive keeps proving it — two Giuseppe Falco, two Carlantonio Morgillo, two Arcangelo Crisci, two Angelo Morgillo, two Gennaro Morgillo, and now three Michele Falco. **VIGLIOTTA is also the surname of the strada Costa Giuseppe Falco's wife, Gelsomina.** Two Falco–Vigliotta marriages in one small town is worth noticing and nothing more.

what: a churchman in a family of day-labourers

what: a nun and two Falco-Falco marriages, all from an index and none from an act

what: a parish attributed, corrected, and now reopened

AGNETIS Virginis et Martyris TERRAE ARGENTII»**: the parish of **Sant'Agnese in Arienzo**, with acts of **1843**. A film label covers a whole reel and a reel can hold several parishes.

what: a granddaughter of the founder, and her household reassembled from two archives
was: Giuseppe Falco and Antonia di Guida were held as the parents of **two infants** and, since this morning, of **Don Giovanni the deacon**.

what: the husband of an isolate, documented at last
was: **MARGHERITA FALCO** was an isolate — a name from a fragment of a parish baptism, «dominico Crisci e Margaria Falco», with nothing attached to it.
now: **DOMENICO CRISCI, «VEDOVO DI MARGHERITA FALCO», died 9 January 1855 at Arienzo, aged EIGHTY**, a *contadino* of **STRADA CRISCI**, **son of the late VINCENZO CRISCI and the late MARIA DI LUCIA**. So Margherita Falco **died before January 1855**, and her husband was born about **1775**.
how: The 1855 Arienzo death register, which has no index at either end, read act by act.
why: Whose daughter Margherita was is **still unknown**. A woman married to a man born about 1775 was probably born in the same decade, which would put her in Matteo Falco's generation or the next — **but that is arithmetic, not evidence, and it is left as arithmetic.**

what: a second Falco family at Arienzo, with a nun and a priest in it
was: For four years this archive has read **every Falco found at Arienzo as a possible relation**, and the *Don* before a name was treated as a curiosity.
now: **DON FRANCESCO FALCO and DONNA MADDALENA STELLATO** had **a daughter in a convent and a son in orders**: **Donna Angela Maria Falco, *monaca***, died 14 November 1850, and **Don Giacomo Falco, *sacerdote***, died 20 June 1857. A *Don* for a father, a *Donna* for a mother. **No kinship to this line is claimed or suspected.**
how: The Arienzo death indexes of 1850 and 1857. Index entries only — **neither act has been read**.
why: It settles something the archive had been half-assuming. **The surname carries at least two social worlds in one small town**, and probably two unrelated stocks. What identifies people here is the **street, the trade, the parish and the spouse** — never the name. \n\nAnd a near-miss worth recording: **Don Giovanni Falco the deacon, who died in 1849, is NOT of this house.** His father is **Giuseppe Falco, *colono* of strada Camellara** — the founder's own son. A labourer's boy and a gentleman's boy, both in orders, in the same parish, eight years apart. They were nearly filed together on the strength of the «Don».

what: fifteen consecutive years of Arienzo deaths, and the man who is not in them
was: **GIUSEPPE FALCO**, the founder's son, last seen alive in **April 1854** at about seventy-four.
now: **He is in none of the death registers of 1844 to 1858.** Fifteen consecutive years read — 1848 and 1855 act by act, because they have **no index at all**, and the rest through their *tavole*. Every Falco in those fifteen years is now listed on the site, with the act read where it matters.
how: Antenati, `an_ua14346`–`an_ua14360`. The index format changes almost every year: a separate volume to 1849, bound into the register from 1850, alphabetical by surname to 1853, **by act number in 1854**, absent in 1855, and alphabetical by letter-section from 1856.
why: Recorded as a method note so the shape of the negative is on the record, not just its conclusion. **Fifteen years of not finding a man is worth publishing only if the reader can see exactly which years were read and how.**

what: an infant's year, missing until the baptism ten days before was found
was: A parish burial: «**Raphael Falco filius Josephi e Antonia di Guida, infans**», dated **26 February** — **with no year**, and carried on the site that way.
now: **Born 16 February 1811, buried 26 February 1811 — TEN DAYS OLD.** The baptism is on the same leaf, and the margin beside it reads «**Raphael Falco obiit die 26 Februarii 1811**».
how: A sweep of the Arienzo parish baptisms for «Antonia di Guida», which returned five children of Giuseppe Falco this archive did not have.
why: Recorded because the fix came from the same page the problem was on. The burial note and the baptism were **ten days and two lines apart**, and the archive had one without the other for weeks.

what: a fifth stated age overturned by a baptism, in one week
was: **DON GIOVANNI FALCO, DIACONO**, «di anni **VENTICINQUE**» in his death act of 26 November 1849 — so born about 1824.
now: **Baptised in APRIL 1825** — «baptizavit infantem natum ex Josepho Falco, et Antonia di Guida … cui dedit nomen Joannes». **He was TWENTY-FOUR.**
how: Arienzo parish baptisms via FamilySearch's full-text. **Machine transcription — the image has not been read, and the day is not legible in it.**
why: The fifth in a week: Vincenzo (1792), Gioacchino (1779), Chiara Rivetti (1766), the «about 1775» of the first Gioacchino, and now Giovanni. **A stated age in these registers is an estimate, and this archive now treats it as one.** Published at transcription strength: if the day were read as March the arithmetic would still give twenty-four, so the conclusion survives the uncertainty — which is why it is published at all.

what: a daughter found in 1797 that puts this morning's correction under strain
was: This morning the archive **corrected Gioacchino Falco's age**: «born about 1775» from his death act's stated seventy-six, replaced by a **baptism of 2 February 1779**, making him **seventy-two**.

how: A sweep of the Arienzo parish baptisms. **Machine transcription — the image has not been read.**
why: **Published as an open question, not a reversal.** Three readings fit and none is established: he married very young; or the 1797 father is a **different** Gioacchino Falco, in a town with two or three Falco stocks; or the 1777 marginal *obiit* belongs to a neighbouring entry and the 1774 boy lived after all — the least likely, since the cross and the name were read at magnification side by side. **Nothing has been moved on the strength of it.** What would settle it: the 1797 image, and Gioacchino and Vittoria's marriage act, which the parish marriage index locates at «Joachim Falco fol 19».

what: a fourth child, and a mother's surname the archive did not have
was: **Gioacchino / Guglielmo Falco** and **Andreana** — three children born at Arienzo, **Raffaela 1880, Giovanni 1883, Carmina 1891** — the mother carried with **no surname**.
now: A parish baptism «ex legittimis coniugibus **JOACHIM FALCO et ANDREANA CRISCI**, cui dedi nomen **CARMELA**» — **a fourth child**, and the mother is a **CRISCI**.
how: The same parish sweep. **Transcription only; the image has not been read and the year on that leaf is not legible** — the machine offers 1591, 159 and 1897 for the acts around it.
why: Published at transcription strength because the **name and the surname are the finding** and neither depends on the date. The year is left blank rather than guessed.

what: the founder's death window, cut from «sometime before 1809» to seven years
was: **MATTEO FALCO** — «died by 8 December 1814, probably before 1809». The earliest document naming him, of 1814, calls his son «Pasquale Falco **del fu** Matteo».
now: **He was ALIVE on 16 May 1796 and again on 4 August 1802.** Both his children's marriage acts call them «filium Matthei, et Franciscae Crisci» — **with no «quondam» before either parent** — and **this scribe uses «quondam»**: on the very same 1802 leaf he writes «Carolum Antonium Morgillo filium **quondam** Caroli Antonii, et Emiliae», father dead and mother living. **So Matteo Falco died between August 1802 and 1809**, and his death is in the **Arienzo parish death register** for those seven years.
how: The marriage of his son Gioacchino, 16 May 1796, read from the image — found by searching the parish marriage collection for the bride's surname rather than the groom's.
why: **It is an argument from silence, and this archive distrusts those more than anything.** It is published with the evidence for the scribe's own practice attached, because that is the difference between an argument and a guess — and it is labelled as strong evidence, not proof. What it buys is precision: the question that has run for months is now **seven years in one register in one parish.**

what: an open question closed, and this morning's correction reinforced
was: Published this afternoon as **open**: a daughter baptised to «Joachimo Falco e Victoria Cemmino» in **1797** would make our Gioacchino a father at eighteen — or mean the 1797 father was **a different Gioacchino Falco**.
now: **Their marriage act, 16 May 1796, names the groom «JOACHIM FALCO FILIUM MATTHEI, ET FRANCISCAE CRISCI».** The «different Gioacchino» reading is **eliminated**. He married at **seventeen years and three months**, and was a father at eighteen. The alternative — that our man was the FIRST Joachim of 1774, who would have been twenty-one — stays closed by that entry's own margin: a drawn cross and «obiit die 11 Decembris 1777».
how: The parish marriage register, read from the image.
why: **This morning's correction stands and is better supported than when it was made: Gioacchino was SEVENTY-TWO in 1851, not seventy-six.** A clerk guessing an old man's age would reach for the number that fits a man who married at twenty-one. He married at seventeen. \n\nThe question was published as open for about four hours. That is how it should work.

what: a burial that would close the founder's death window — and the arithmetic that stops it
was: Nothing. **MATTEO FALCO's death** is placed between **August 1802 and 1809**, seven years, on the strength of the missing «quondam» in his children's marriage acts.
now: The Arienzo parish death register carries «**FRANCISCA CRISCI, VIDUA [q.m …] FALCO**, aetatis suae annorum **ottanta circiter** … **31 December 1805**», buried in the confraternity of **Santa Maria delle Grazie**. If she is the founder's wife, **Matteo died between August 1802 and December 1805** and the window closes to three and a half years.

what: a fourth death in one house, and two records joining

A marriage read this morning and a death read this afternoon, found by different methods in different archives, turning out to be one family.

what: the third «Falco–Falco» couple dissolves, and a child's death moves two years

now: **The act says «figlio di FRANCESCO … e di RAFFAELA FALCO», and it is dated 14 August 1853.** So the third Falco–Falco couple is **the same household as the other two** — Francesco and Raffaela — and **all three index entries were one family**. And Clemente died **14 August 1853**, not 1855: same day, same month, same age, same parents. **The parish entry and the civil act are one death**, and the machine's «1855» is wrong.
how: Arienzo, Morti 1853, atto 46, read from the image — including a zoom on «quattordici … Agosto» because the year was load-bearing.
why: **Three index entries produced three apparent Falco–Falco marriages. All three were the same couple, and the index misread the mother's name each time.** Not one of the four this archive published this afternoon survives as a separate household. \n\nAnd the date matters for more than tidiness: **Clemente died before his mother, not after.** The house on strada Camellara lost a two-year-old in 1850, a five-year-old in 1853, the mother in 1854 and a three-year-old in 1855.

what: the archive's central question, answered — and the argument published four hours earlier, refuted
was: **MATTEO FALCO**, head of this line: «died by 8 December 1814, probably before 1809». Then, this afternoon and at length: «**both alive on 4 August 1802**», and «died between August 1802 and 1809» — argued from the **absence of «quondam»** in his children's marriage acts, with the same scribe's use of «filium **quondam** Caroli Antonii» on the very same leaf offered as the warrant.
now: **HE DIED ON 18 JULY 1802.** Arienzo parish death register: «Anno Domini Millesimo Octingentesimo **SECUNDO 1802**, die vero **DECIMA OCTAVA 18 JULII**, **MATTHEUS FALCO, VIR FRANCISCAE CRISCI** … omnibus Sacramentis munitus … obiit, et **in Archipresbyterali Coemeterio ejus cadaver humatum est**.» **When his son Giuseppe married on 4 August he had been dead for seventeen days**, and the act still says «filium Matthei» with no «quondam».
how: A sweep of the parish death collection for Falco on pages naming Arienzo, filtered to the 1800s — the same corpus that produced the 1805 widow lead an hour earlier.
why: **The refutation is the finding, not a footnote to it.** The argument from silence was careful, it carried its evidence, it was labelled strong evidence rather than proof — and it was **wrong at both ends**. In these registers a missing «quondam» means nothing, even when the same scribe uses it correctly two acts away. \n\nIt also dates the summer of 1802 exactly: **Rosa married on 12 July**, six days before her father died; **he died on 18 July**; **Giuseppe married on 4 August**, seventeen days after burying him. Both marriages are on one leaf of the marriage register, read this morning in the belief that he was alive at both.

what: a surname left unread this morning, supplied by a death act this evening
was: The 1802 marriage of **Rosa Falco** and **Carlo Antonio Morgillo** names the groom «filium **quondam** Caroli Antonii, et **EMILIAE** …» — and this archive published that **the mother's surname could not be read**: «the scan is 2,258 pixels across the whole leaf, and that one word does not survive the magnification».
now: **It is RIVETTI.** Carlo Antonio Morgillo's own death entry, **17 June 1842**, aged **sixty**: «**filius q[uonda]m Caroli Antonii, et q[uonda]m MARIA RIVETTI, ac VIDUUS ROSAE FALCO**», buried **in the church of San Giovanni**. The two acts name her Emilia and Maria; the **surname** is the finding.
how: A sweep of the parish death collection — the same corpus that gave up Matteo Falco's own death an hour earlier. **Transcription only; the image has not been read.**
why: Recorded because **the answer came from the opposite end of the man's life**. The archive spent an hour on the 1802 leaf trying to enlarge one word; the word was legible forty years later in his own burial. **When a name will not come off one act, look for the same person's other acts.** \n\nAnd **RIVETTI again**: generation three married a Chiara Rivetti, Antonia di Guida's mother was a Magdalena Rivetta, and now Rosa Falco's mother-in-law. The name is everywhere in this parish and still proves nothing on its own.

what: the founder's birth year, on evidence for the first time
was: **MATTEO FALCO, born about 1740** — carried since the beginning of this archive, inferred from nothing better than the date of his first known child.
now: **About 1747.** His death act, read from the image: «**aetatis suae annorum 55 circiter**», 18 July 1802.
how: The act itself, at magnification, after the machine transcription garbled the number.
why: **Fifty-five fits everything and 1740 never had to.** He fathered children from 1767 to 1786 — from twenty to thirty-nine — and married by 1766 at about nineteen. *The figure is written «55» in a hand whose two glyphs are identical; the second could be an 8, so the archive says **about fifty-five, born about 1744–1747**.*

what: the 1805 widow's age — my over-read corrected by the image, in the other direction
was: This afternoon this archive read «annorum **ottanta** circiter» in the 1805 burial of «Francisca Crisci, vidua … Falco», built an objection on it, then **withdrew the reading** as an over-read of an illegible machine word.
now: **The image says «annorum 70 circiter» — SEVENTY.** Neither the eighty first published nor simply unknowable. Born about **1735**.
how: The act read at magnification in a browser FamilySearch had not blocked.
why: Recorded because it leaves the question **harder, not easier**. Seventy in 1805 makes her **fifty-one** at the 1786 birth that is documented as hers, and **twelve years older** than Matteo Falco, who was about fifty-five in 1802. Both are possible and neither is comfortable. **The word after «vidua» is still unread**, and it is still the whole question.

what: the founder's wife, found — and an age got wrong three times in one day
was: «FRANCISCA CRISCI, VIDUA […] FALCO», 31 December 1805 — published this afternoon as **a lead only**, because the word after «vidua» was rendered «Manel» by the machine and «everything turns on it». Her age was read as **eighty**, then withdrawn, then read from the image as **seventy**.
now: **«FRANCISCA CRISCI VIDUA MAT‑THEI FALCO, aetatis suae annorum 60 circiter»** — read from the image. **It is Matteo's widow.** The surname breaks across the line, «Vidua Mat‑ / thei Falco», which is exactly why the machine could not hold it together. She died **31 December 1805**, aged about **sixty**, and is buried in the **confraternity of Santa Maria delle Grazie**.
how: The act itself, anchored on its own margin label instead of on a horizontal band of the page.
why:
**The age was wrong three times before it was right, and the three ways it was wrong are the finding.** «Eighty» was my over-read of a garbled machine word. «Seventy» was read correctly off the image — **from the entry below**, which is Francesca CILLO, wife of Vincenzo Laudato, who died on 1 January 1806. «Sixty» is the act. 

**Reading a horizontal band of a register page is not reading an entry.** Twice in one afternoon a number was taken from a neighbour's line. **Anchor on the margin label and on the entry's own first and last words.** 

And with it the founding couple closes at both ends: **he died 18 July 1802 at about fifty-five, she on 31 December 1805 at about sixty** — born about 1747 and 1745. She bore her last child at about forty-one and was about two years older than him. **Nothing about them is strange any more**, which is itself the confirmation.

what: the FindMyPast verdict was measured from outside the paywall, and it was too strong

now: They contain **six** records of this family, all passenger lists. Beside the 1964 arrival: **FILOMENA FALCO, 5 February 1968** (NAA barcode 9788535, p. 251) and **CARMINANTONIO FALCO, 19 May 1969** (barcode 12211391, p. 1711), with a second crossing under «Carminatonio» on **24 July 1972** (barcode 12047001, p. 1605). **A first-name filter that returns zero is not a nil.** «carm» returned nothing; «carminantonio» returned the record. The September sweep read what a signed-out session was shown and wrote the verdict as though it had read the holding.

FindMyPast's whole holding for this family is passenger lists. It is six records deep, not one. 

And the answer to «is there a FindMyPast tree?» is **no** — the account has none, and the family tree lives on MyHeritage.

On the face of the name that is a breach of the rule that **living people are named and nothing more**, and the entry was about to be pulled.

The 1964 arrival is tree id 4000025 — **born at Forchia on 8 June 1930, generation eight, David's wife's grandfather** — whom `tools/build_living.py` had already excluded from the living list as an ancestor, and whose death in **2026** the direct line already recorded. **Nothing was published in breach and nothing needed pulling.**

Identity lives in the data, not the markup.*» The gate was built to stop a leak; the near-miss here ran the other way — **a name-level check was about to delete a true fact about a dead man.** \n\n**Redaction needs identification just as much as publication does.** A rule enforced on names alone will both leak and over-delete, and the second failure is quieter than the first because nobody complains about a fact that vanished.

what: generation four's CIVIL marriage act is not where it has to be
was: The church act is settled: **Raffaele Falco married Angela Rosa Morgillo on 5 March 1844 at Sant'Agnese, Arienzo.** Under the Two Sicilies that wedding must have a civil counterpart — a *solenne promessa* before the sindaco, with the priest's certificate of the celebration facing it. **That act names both fathers and both mothers, with ages, trades and streets.** It is the richest document this family could still recover.
now: **It is not in the register.** Arienzo *Matrimoni* 1844 (`an_ua14248`, 32 images) has been **read end to end** — exactly **29 acts, 6 January to 30 December**, closing with the Procuratore del Re's certificate — and **no Falco appears in any of them**, as groom, bride or parent. Acts 29–35 of 1843 (`an_ua14247`, 8 Oct – 28 Dec) were read as well. **No Falco.** Neither volume has an index; that was checked, not assumed.
how: Every act's name band rendered from the Antenati images and read. The acts are published in full at `data/arienzo-civil-marriages-1843-1844.tsv`, three of them marked NOT SECURELY READ rather than guessed.
why: **A negative is only worth what its boundaries are worth**, so here they are. What remains untested: the first twenty-eight acts of 1843; San Felice a Cancello, the bride's comune of birth; and the plain possibility that no civil act was ever drawn. \n\n**And a caution that may matter more than the search.** Every act in the 1843 volume reads «*comune di CORPO D'ARIENZO*»; every act in the 1844 volume reads «*comune di Arienzo*». Both are catalogued under the one heading "Arienzo". This archive **does not yet know** whether that is a second comune or just how one clerk styled the town — but until it does, **no 1843 nil can be said to cover both**. Several of this archive's published eliminations run through that year.

what: four generations of MAJONE joined from two sources that never met
was: The 1839 death sweep held **FILIPPO MAJONE, 70, contadino, «marito di Maria Martini», strada Capodiconca, d. 16 November 1839**, son of the late Bartolomeo Majone and Francesca Diglio. It sat there as one more name in a register nobody had a reason to revisit.
now: Reading the 1844 marriage acts turned up **three grooms in six months, all «figlio di Filippo Majone defunto e Maria Martini»** — **Raffaele** (37), **Clemente** (33) and **Bartolomeo** (c. 22). Three brothers marrying five years after their father's death. The house now runs **four generations**: Bartolomeo → Filippo (c. 1769–1839) → Raffaele, Clemente and Bartolomeo.
how: Checking a find against what the archive already held **in the same pass that published it** — the standing rule, and the only reason this was seen at all.
why:
**The corroboration is the naming, not the names.** Filippo's father was BARTOLOMEO and Filippo's son is BARTOLOMEO — the Neapolitan custom working as it should, which independently supports a reading («Maria Martini») that went in marked `[?]`. The ages fit without strain. 

**What is not claimed:** Giovanna Majone, 27, who married in June 1844 «figlia di … Majone defunto», may be a fourth child of this house; her father's forename was not read with confidence, so she is not entered as one. 

**And it moves a standing question.** The queue asks whether the Majone of Arienzo and the Majone of Arpaia are one kindred. **Two of Filippo's three sons are recorded living toward Arpaia while the third stayed in Arienzo** — the place-name marked `[?]` and not yet proven. If it holds they are not a separate kindred but Arienzo sons who moved eight kilometres up the valley: **the same short-range drift the Falco made two generations later**, when Raffaele Falco's last child was born at Arpaia in 1913.

what: the founders' «unnamed daughter» was a woman this archive already knew
was: The children of Matteo Falco and Francesca Crisci were listed with **«a daughter, name not legible (machine gives «proja»), baptised 5 January 1786»** — an unidentified infant, counted as a child in her own right. **Rosa Falco was listed separately**, from a burial and a marriage.
now: **They are the same person, and her name is ROSA MARIA.** The act reads «*baptizavit infantem **NATAM** ex **MATTHEO FALCO**, et **FRANCISCA CRISCI** Conjugibus hujus Parochiae, **que nominata est ROSA MARIA***», the celebrant **Canonico SABBATINO CRISCI, sostituto**. So the founders had **one child fewer** than the archive was counting, and one more woman with a whole life attached: **Rosa Maria Falco married Carlo Antonio Morgillo on 12 July 1802** and **died on strada Camellara on 16 October 1830**, «*d'anni quarantadue*».
how: Read from the image at `3Q9M-CSD3-13XZ-1` — «proja» was the machine's attempt at «Rosa Maria».
why: **And it moved a citation.** Her baptism was cited to `3Q9M-CSD3-13XB-R`, an ark taken from machine-parsed text whose own extract runs «*Angelis Porrino … 1793 … Rosa Falco … 1808*» — three dates that cannot all belong to one 1786 act. **The act is on `13XZ-1`, which has now been read.** What is actually on `13XB-R` has NOT been checked and no claim is made about it. \n\n**The stated age does not quite fit and is published anyway.** Baptised January 1786 she would be **forty-four** in October 1830, not forty-two. This archive has already documented that the Arienzo clerks guessed ages — a two-year gap is inside the noise, and saying so is better than quietly choosing the reading that tidies it.

what: the founders' last «unnamed» child was the first Gioacchino, and the year was wrong by three
was: The reconstructed household carried **«[unnamed] — child — baptism — 25 Nov 1777»**, cited to `3Q9M-CSD3-13H2-1`, as a child in its own right. **Separately** the archive held **«the first Gioacchino, baptised 25 November 1774, obiit 11 December 1777»** — from the same ark.
now: **One act, one child.** Read from the image: «*Anno Domini Millesimo septingentesimo septuagesimo qua[rto] … die vero **VIGESIMAQUINTA 25 NOVEMBRIS** … Canonicus **BRUNO** Substituens baptizavit … ex **MATTHEO FALCO**, et **FRANCISCA CRISCI** Conjugibus*», the margin reading **«Joachim Falco — OBIIT DIE 11 DECEMBRIS 1777»**. The year is **1774**, the day 25 November, and the child is **JOACHIM**. The «25 Nov 1777» row was the same act with the year out by three.
how: The act read at native resolution, **and the year line read on its own** rather than inferred from the act above it. The archive has been wrong before by taking a number from a neighbouring line, so the year was fetched as a separate crop even though the answer looked obvious.
why: **With this the founders' children are complete and every one of them is named**: Pasquale (1767), Francisca Anna Angela (1771), Giuseppe, **Joachim (1774–1777)**, **Gioacchino (1779)** and **Rosa Maria (1786)**. Two «unnamed children» have been dissolved in one day and **both turned out to be people the archive already knew**. \n\nAnd the naming is now documented at both ends from the images: **Joachim died on 11 December 1777 and the name was given again on 2 February 1779**, fourteen months later. This family named children after their dead — it did so again with the two Giovannas — and that is no longer an inference.

what: the CORPO D'ARIENZO warning, raised and withdrawn on the same day
was: Reading the **back** of the 1843 marriage volume, every act said «*comune di **CORPO D'ARIENZO***» while every act of 1844 said «*comune di **Arienzo***», both catalogued under the one heading. **A warning went up here this morning**: that a sweep eliminating "Arienzo" for a year might have covered only one of two jurisdictions — which would have undercut several of this archive's published eliminations.
now: **Reading the same volume from the FRONT settles it.** Acts **1, 2 and 3** of 1843 say «*comune di **ARIENZO***». **Act 4 and everything after says «comune di CORPO D'ARIENZO»** — and acts 3 and 4 are three weeks apart, **before the same officer, RAFFAELE DE MIERI, sindaco, in the same book.** One comune, two ways of writing it. **The warning is withdrawn.**
how: Reading the volume end to end instead of sampling it — which was going to happen anyway for a different reason.
why: **The warning is left standing on this page rather than deleted, because raising it was right.** On the evidence available at the time — seven consecutive acts, all saying Corpo d'Arienzo — the honest move was to flag that every 1843 nil might be worth less than it looked. **It cost one morning of doubt and bought certainty about fifteen years of eliminations.** \n\nThe likely sense of *corpo* is the ordinary administrative one, the main built-up body of a comune as against its outlying casali, as in *Corpo di Cava*. **That reading is offered, not proved.** What is proved is that it is not a second jurisdiction.

what: sixty-four marriage acts, two whole years, and no Falco at all
was: This morning the archive could say only that **1844 held no Falco marriage** and that acts 29–35 of 1843 held none either — leaving open the possibility that generation four's civil act sat in the earlier part of 1843.
now: **It does not.** Arienzo *Matrimoni* **1843** (`an_ua14247`) is now **read end to end** as well — **35 acts, 1 January to 28 December**. With 1844's 29 acts that is **sixty-four consecutive marriage acts across two whole years, and not one Falco in any role** — groom, bride, or parent of either.
how: Every act's name band rendered from the Antenati images and read. All sixty-four are published in `data/arienzo-civil-marriages-1843-1844.tsv`, uncertain words marked `[?]`.
why: **Two possibilities are left and the archive is not choosing between them.** Either the act is at **SAN FELICE A CANCELLO**, the bride's comune of birth — though the priest at Sant'Agnese called her «*mea Parochiana*» in 1844, so she was living in Arienzo by then — or **no civil act was ever drawn**, which is not as strange as it sounds in a town whose church and civil registers plainly did not always speak to each other. \n\n**What the sixty-four acts did give** is a whole working town: four more households on **strada Camellara**, a **fourth child** of the Majone house, and the confirmation of a name that had gone in marked uncertain.

what: generation four's civil marriage act — found, hours after this archive said it was not there
was: **This morning this archive published**, after reading sixty-four Arienzo marriage acts of 1843 and 1844 end to end: «*generation four's civil marriage act is not where it must be*» — with **San Felice a Cancello listed as untested possibility number one.**
now: **It was there.** **San Felice a Cancello, *Matrimoni* 1844, atto 12, 7 MARCH 1844** (`an_ua50256`, image 13): «*… sono comparsi nella Casa Comunale **RAFFAELE FALCO** di anni **ventisei**, nato in **ARIENZO CORPO**, di professione **contadino**, domiciliato **strada CAMMELLARA**, figlio di **VINCENZO FALCO** di professione simile, domiciliato **ivi**, e di **ANDREANA CRISCI** di professione **filatrice**, domiciliata **ivi**; e **ANGELA ROSA MORGILLO** di anni **ventisei**, contadina, **nata in questo Comune**, figlia di **ORAZIO MORGILLO**, colono, e di **VINCENZA PESCE**, contadina*».
how: Reading the bride's comune instead of the groom's. **The civil promise is made where the BRIDE lives** — the ordinary rule, and the one this archive had not applied.
why:
**VINCENZO FALCO WAS ALIVE ON 7 MARCH 1844** — no *defunto*, «domiciliato **ivi**», on strada Cammellara beside his son. Generation three had been traced only to his baptism in 1792 and his marriage in December 1814; **this is thirty years later and it is the latest date the archive has for him.** Andreana Crisci is alive too, a spinner on the same street, and so are Orazio Morgillo and Vincenza Pesce at San Felice. 

**The Arienzo sweep was not wasted** — it is what proves the act is not at Arienzo, and it produced the Majone household and six Camellara households on the way. **But the reasoning that made Arienzo obvious was wrong, and it was wrong because the archive assumed the groom's town.** 

**And a four-day gap is published rather than tidied away.** The parish act gives the marriage as **5 March**; the civil column certifies the celebration on **9 March**. Both are read from images, they do not agree, and no attempt is made here to choose between them.

what: there is more than one FORCHIA — and the archive has been searching the right one
was: «Forchia» has been treated throughout as **one place**: the comune in the province of **Benevento**, beside Arpaia, where **Filomena Annecchino was born on 10 April 1897**. Her birth act has been hunted there across FamilySearch and Antenati for weeks and never found.
now: **There is also FORCHIA DI CERVINO, a frazione of Cervino in the province of Caserta**, about fifteen kilometres west — and **this archive's own sources name it outright.** The Arienzo parish pages carry «*contratto matrimonio nella cura di **Forchia di Cervino***» and «*contratto matrimonio in **Forchia di Cervino** il dì 28 Agosto*». The registers also write **«FORCHIA D'ARPAIA»** and **«FORCHIA DI CERVINARA»**, Cervinara being in Avellino; whether those are two further places or clerks' ways of pointing at the first two is **not settled**.

what: generation six's marriage dossier, opened — and it documents the line a generation deeper

**It is the PROCESSETTI**, and generation six's fascicolo is open: **«1897 — Registro dei Matrimoni — FALCO RAFFAELE · MAIONE COSTANZA — Numero 41, Parte 1ª — DOCUMENTI INCLUSI N. SEI»**, with banns published on **12 and 19 September 1897**.

what: a daughter for generation five, and both of Costanza Maione's parents
